title: Reduction of in utero lead exposures in South African populations: Positive impact of unleaded petrol.
ehr_evidence: Lead was measured in the maternal blood, urine and cord blood using Inductive Coupled Plasma Mass spectrometry (ICP-MS); neonate characteristics (birth weight, length, head circumference, gestational age) were retrieved from hospital medical records and socio-demographic data from a questionnaire.
summary: Cross-sectional study of 640 pregnant women delivering at public hospitals in South Africa measuring maternal blood, cord blood, and urine lead levels and examining birth outcomes and contributing socio-economic/lifestyle factors.
key_findings: Overall geometric mean maternal blood lead (PbB) was 1.32 μg/dL (n = 640; 95% CI, 1.24–1.40).
Maternal PbB was significantly higher in Indian Ocean vs Atlantic Ocean residents (GM 1.73 vs 0.95 μg/dL; Wilcoxon rank sum, p<0.001).
Positive correlation between log maternal PbB and log cord blood Pb (rho = 0.65, p<0.001).
In female neonates, a positive association was found between cord blood Pb and head circumference (rho = 0.243; p<0.016).
No significant association was found between maternal PbB and infant birth weight, length, or head circumference.

In the final multivariate model, non-use of pesticides at home was associated with lower PbB (β = -0.14; 95% CI, -0.26 to -0.02); secondary (β = -0.28; 95% CI, -0.49 to -0.064) and tertiary (β = -0.25; 95% CI, -0.47 to -0.03) education were associated with lower PbB.
4.4% (n = 14) of cord blood samples had a lead level >5 μg/dL and 1.3% (n = 4) >10 μg/dL.
pathologies_diseases: Birth outcomes (gestational age, birth length, head circumference, Apgar score, birth weight)
population: 640 pregnant women delivering at public hospitals in KwaZulu-Natal and Western Cape provinces, South Africa (mean age ~25 years)
limitations: Recall bias in dietary intake data.
Cord blood sampling was limited to Indian Ocean coast sites only due to financial constraints, introducing potential bias.
